title: Krishna's dinner at Vidura's
hookLine: Krishna turns down a palace feast for a meal given with love; sattvic food
carry: sattvic food: simple, and given with love
last: A FAST IS A VOW, CHOSEN WITH LOVE.

cards: Krishna rides into the capital as a messenger of peace, trying to stop a war between cousins. Prince Duryodhana, who wants that war, has laid out a royal welcome: rich dishes, fine seats, every comfort.
Krishna won't eat a bite. A guest eats someone's food for one of two reasons, he says: because there is love, or because he is in need. You have no love for me, and I'm not in need.
Then he walks to the house of Vidura, his honest friend, and eats there, gladly.

teach.b: That's the Mahabharata. Families still retell it, sometimes with extra loving details of their own. The teaching under it runs all through Hindu kitchens: food carries more than taste.
Krishna himself sorts the world into three qualities, the gunas. Sattva is clarity, balance, light. Rajas is drive and restlessness.
Tamas is heaviness and dullness. And he sorts food the same way. Sattvic food, he says, is fresh, wholesome and nourishing, and increases life, strength, health and joy.
Rajasic food is too sour, too salty, too hot and burning, and brings pain and unease. Tamasic food is stale, spoiled, or left over too long.
In practice, sattvic is often taken to mean fresh, simple, vegetarian meals, and some also skip onion and garlic. Families and communities differ, and not every Hindu is vegetarian.
But many Hindus add what Krishna showed at Vidura's door: the heart of the cook and the giver goes into the meal.

That's why some grandmothers won't let anyone cook angry, why temple kitchens are kept calm and clean, and why many families offer the food to God first, so it comes back as prasad. So sattvic isn't just a menu.
Before you eat, ask two things. Will this leave me clearer?

teach.h: SATTVIC FOOD: SIMPLE, AND GIVEN WITH LOVE.
teach.b: And was it given with love?

how: Many Hindus aim for sattvic meals, fresh, simple and often vegetarian, cooked with a calm mind and offered to God before eating; some also avoid onion, garlic and alcohol, especially on festival days, fast days or in temple kitchens; practices differ widely by family and community.

o: full of clarity: leaving the mind calm
spicy food that fires up your energy

games.q: the feast and the gunas — tap the pairs.
p: the honest friend whose meal Krishna ate

s: Krishna ate Duryodhana's feast to keep the peace
he refused it: there was no love in it, and he wasn't in need. he ate at Vidura's.
Krishna sorts food by the three gunas
sattvic, rajasic and tamasic: fresh and nourishing, burning and harsh, or stale.
all Hindus eat the same sattvic diet
families and communities differ, and not every Hindu is vegetarian.

games.q: you've made a fresh, healthy dinner, but you're furious, cooking it while arguing on the phone. by the teaching of sattva, what's missing?
o: a calm, loving heart: what you cook with goes into the meal.
games.why: Krishna turned down a feast without love. for many Hindus, the cook's heart goes into the food, so sattvic means how it's made, not just what's in it.

practice: If there's a small bite near you, a piece of fruit, a nut, a sip of tea, take it now; if not, picture your next meal. Before you eat, look at it and ask where it came from and whose hands made it.
If you pray, offer it silently to God first, as many Hindus do. If you don't, thank whoever made it. Then eat one bite slowly, and notice how you feel: clearer, heavier, or the same.

wordCard.voice: Sattvic. Full of sattva, clarity: simple, fresh food, given with love, that leaves the mind clear. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit sāttvika: of sattva, the quality of clarity, goodness and balance.

carryVoice: Your line: sattvic food: simple, and given with love. Krishna chose Vidura's table over a palace. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Krishna's peace mission: he declines Duryodhana's hospitality and is received at Vidura's house)
Bhagavad Gita 17.8–10 (foods dear to the sattvic, rajasic and tamasic)
Bhagavad Gita 14.5–10 (the three gunas born of nature, each prevailing in turn)
